qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

The JACOP 2025 campaign on safety helmets for professional use reveals that 19 of the 65 products examined failed at least one technical test. Thirteen – 20% – did not meet the impact-absorption requirements. The failures were observed following various storage conditions, with the report noting that they occurred particularly frequently after exposure to high or low temperatures. These findings come at a time when the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work is warning that workers are being increasing exposed to extreme heat and other major climaterelated risks. In 2023 workplace accidents claimed the lives of 3 298 workers across the EU, nearly a quarter of whom were in the construction sector. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

Whether it intends to strengthen the requirements and testing protocols applicable to professional personal protective equipment to ensure its effectiveness in conditions of extreme temperatures, which have become more frequent as a result of climate change?

Given the findings of JACOP 2025, how could the Commission help tighten up inspections, expedite the removal of personal protective equipment posing a serious or high risk, and ensure its traceability?

Whether it intends, as part of the forthcoming legislation on quality jobs, to improve coordination between, and increase the staffing levels of, national inspectorates with a view to the more effective enforcement of rules on personal protective equipment and the protection of workers exposed to extreme temperatures?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.11.2026) Pursuant to Directive 89/656/EEC1, personal protective equipment (PPE) must comply with EU safety and health rules on design and manufacture. PPE must be appropriate for the risks involved without itself increasing risk2. Before choosing PPE, employers must assess, inter alia, the characteristics needed for its effectiveness, considering any risks the equipment itself may create3. PPE standards generally include temperature-related performance requirements and testing protocols, where temperature can affect safety or performance. That is the case for the standard EN 397:2012+A1:2012 for industrial safety helmets used in the Joint Actions on Compliance of Products (JACOP25)4. Member States must ensure adequate controls and supervision of the provisions transposing EU occupational safety and health (OSH) directives5, including the PPE Directive. They have a margin of discretion as regards the modalities of such controls. While market surveillance is a competence of national authorities, the upcoming European Product Act proposal aims to strengthen the EU horizontal framework for market surveillance, close accountability gaps, improve traceability of economic operators, and boost enforcement. Coordination and cooperation between national labour inspectorates regarding EU OSH directives are primarily ensured by the Senior Labour Inspectors’ Committee. Member States determine national labour inspectorate staffing levels. EU OSH directives on construction, mining and fishing6 contain detailed provisions on indoor temperature and inclement weather. As part of the envisaged Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is considering updating the Workplace Directive7 to better address risks arising from extreme temperature and extreme weather events at work, among other issues.
1 Council Directive 89/656/EEC on the minimum health and safety requirements for the use by workers of

personal protective equipment at the workplace, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A31989L0656. 2 Article 4(1)(a) of the PPE Directive. 3 Article 4(5) of the PPE Directive. 4 The standard requires mandatory tests at high (+50 °C) and low (-10 °C) temperatures. Optional tests are required at very high (+150 °C) and very low (– 20 °C or – 30 °C) temperatures for special applications. 5 Article 4 of Council Directive 89/656/EEC. 6 Directive 92/57/EEC (Construction), Directives 92/104/EEC and 92/91/EEC (Mining), and Directive 93/103/EC (Fishing). 7 Council Directive 89/654/EEC concerning the minimum safety and health requirements for the workplace, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1989/654/.
